title: PHP Forms & Databases + Intro to Python
intro: This term you will make websites that remember people and store data in a real database, then meet Python, a language used in many jobs. You will build a School Club Registration app and a Python club counter.
termProject: 'School Club Registration' — a PHP + MySQL CRUD app where students sign up for clubs (Coding, Press, JETS, Drama) using only a nickname and class, plus a Python program that reports which clubs are full.

weeks.title: Forms That Listen: $_POST
weeks.goal: I can build a club sign-up form and read what the user typed with PHP.
weeks.learn: A form is like the register a club secretary passes round: people write, then hand it back. The HTML form sends the answers to the server with method='post'. PHP reads them from $_POST. We clean the text with htmlspecialchars so nobody can sneak in bad code. We only ask for a nickname and club — never personal data.

research.q: Ask 3 classmates: which school club would they join — Coding, Press, JETS or Drama?
research.tip: Tally the answers — these become the club options in your form.

build.task: Make a club sign-up form that greets the student by nickname after they submit.
steps: Write a form with method='post', a nickname box and a club dropdown.
In PHP, check if the form was sent.
Read $_POST and clean it with htmlspecialchars.
Echo a welcome message.

weeks.title: Sessions: The App Remembers You
weeks.goal: I can use a PHP session to remember a student's nickname across pages.
weeks.learn: A session is like the gateman giving you a visitor tag: while you wear it, every office knows who you are. 'session_start()' gives each visitor a tag. We store data in $_SESSION. Other pages can read it until you log out, when 'session_destroy()' takes the tag back.

research.q: Ask the school gateman or a security guard: how do they know who a visitor is once inside?
research.tip: Write their method — a session works the same way online.

build.task: Make a page that remembers the club member's nickname and has a logout link.
steps: Call session_start() at the very top.
When the form is sent, save the nickname in $_SESSION.
If a nickname is saved, greet them.
Add ?logout=1 to destroy the session.

Welcome back, ! 👋

Nickname:

A session is like…
opts: A visitor tag the gateman gives you

weeks.say: I used a PHP session so my club page remembers me, like a visitor tag from the gateman.

trainer.open: When you visit an office, the gateman gives you a tag so everyone knows you're allowed in. Today our site gives tags!
plan: Hand a child a paper 'visitor tag'; they visit 2 'offices' who greet them by name.
Kids build club.php, log in, refresh, then log out.
Share research: how real gatemen track visitors.
lookfor: Refreshes and sees they are still remembered
fix: Puts HTML before session_start()
Say: session_start must be the very first thing, before any text.
Saves the file with a different name than club.php

weeks.title: Cookies: A Note Left in the Browser
weeks.goal: I can set and read a cookie to remember a small choice like a favourite theme.
weeks.learn: A cookie is a tiny note your browser keeps, like a sticky note on the fridge saying 'Bring bread'. 'setcookie' writes the note with an expiry time. Next visit, PHP reads it from $_COOKIE. Sessions live on the server; cookies live in the browser. Never keep secrets or personal data in cookies.

research.q: Ask an adult: when a website asks 'Accept cookies?', what do they usually click and why?
research.tip: Write their answer — it helps you explain cookies to your family.

build.task: Remember a student's favourite club colour with a cookie for 7 days.
steps: Check if a colour was chosen in the link (?c=green).
Save it with setcookie for 7 days.
Read $_COOKIE to set the page background.
Click a colour, close the tab, reopen.

trainer.open: A sticky note on the fridge reminds the family of something small. Cookies are sticky notes for websites!

weeks.title: Databases: The Club Register Book
weeks.goal: I can create a database table and add and read rows with SQL.
weeks.learn: A database is like the school's big register book with neat columns. A table has columns (nickname, club, class) and rows (one per student). SQL is the language we use to talk to it. 'CREATE TABLE' draws the columns, 'INSERT' writes a row, and 'SELECT' reads rows back.

research.q: Ask your class teacher: what columns are in the class register?
research.tip: Write the column names — but for our club table we'll only keep safe ones like nickname and club.

build.task: Create a 'members' table, add 3 club members and read them back.
steps: Write CREATE TABLE with id, nickname, club, class.
INSERT three members.
SELECT all members.
Run it in phpMyAdmin's SQL tab.

check.q: In a table, one student is one…
Which SQL command adds a new row?
What does 'SELECT * FROM members' do?

weeks.say: I used SQL to build a club register table, add members and read them back.

trainer.open: The school register has neat columns and one line per student. Today we build a digital register!
plan: Draw a register table on the board: columns and rows.
Kids run the SQL in phpMyAdmin and add one more member.
Share research: which register columns are safe to store?
props: Lab PC with MySQL and phpMyAdmin
fix: Forgets quotes around text values
Say: words go inside 'single quotes'; numbers don't need them.
Misses the semicolon
Every SQL sentence ends with ; like a full stop.

weeks.title: SQL Detective: WHERE, UPDATE, DELETE
weeks.goal: I can filter, change and remove rows with WHERE, UPDATE and DELETE.
weeks.learn: WHERE is a rule that picks only some rows, like the teacher saying 'only JSS2 stand up'. 'SELECT ... WHERE club = 'Coding'' finds only coders. 'UPDATE' changes a row, like a member moving clubs. 'DELETE' removes a row. Always use WHERE with UPDATE and DELETE, or you change everybody!

research.q: Ask a club patron or teacher: how often do students switch clubs, and how do they record it?
research.tip: Write their answer — that's exactly what UPDATE does.

build.task: Find all Coding members, move Ada to Coding, and remove Kunle.
steps: SELECT with WHERE club = 'Coding'.
UPDATE Ada's club WHERE nickname = 'Ada'.
DELETE WHERE nickname = 'Kunle'.
SELECT again with ORDER BY to check.

check.q: What does WHERE do?
opts: Picks only rows that match a rule

check.q: What happens if you DELETE without WHERE?
Which command changes Ada's club?

weeks.say: I used WHERE to pick only the right rows, and UPDATE and DELETE to change the club register.

trainer.open: If the teacher says 'everyone sit', all sit. If she says 'only JSS2 sit', that's WHERE!
plan: Game: 'Only those in Coding Club, stand up!' — that's WHERE.

Kids run each query and check results.

lookfor: Predicts which rows a query returns
fix: Uses double = (==) in SQL
Say: SQL uses one = for comparing.
Runs DELETE without WHERE

weeks.title: PHP Meets MySQL: PDO Connect & Insert
weeks.goal: I can connect PHP to MySQL with PDO and safely insert a new club member from a form.
weeks.learn: PDO is PHP's bridge to the database, like the Okada that carries messages between two towns. We connect with the database name, user and password. A prepared statement uses '?' placeholders so attackers can't inject bad SQL. Then 'execute' sends the real values. This is the 'C' (Create) in CRUD.

research.q: Ask an adult who works in an office: how do they collect and store sign-up forms now?
research.tip: Write their method — our app replaces the paper pile.

build.task: Connect to the clubs database and insert a new member from the form.
steps: Create a PDO connection in a try block.
Check if the form was posted.
Use a prepared INSERT with ? placeholders.
Show a success message and the form.
build.code: setAttribute(PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE, PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION); } catch (PDOException $e) { die("Database not reachable. Is MySQL running?"); } $msg = ""; if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST" && trim($_POST["nick"]) !== "") { $stmt = $pdo->prepare("INSERT INTO members (nickname, club, class) VALUES (?, ?, ?)"); $stmt->execute([trim($_POST["nick"]), $_POST["club"], $_POST["class"]]); $msg = "Member added! 🎉"; } ?>

check.q: What is PDO?
Why use '?' placeholders?
opts: To stop bad SQL being injected

check.q: Inserting a new row is which letter of CRUD?

weeks.say: I connected PHP to MySQL with PDO and safely added a new club member using placeholders.

trainer.open: An Okada carries messages between two towns. PDO carries data between PHP and MySQL!
plan: Draw two 'towns' (PHP and MySQL) and a road (PDO) between them.

Say: never glue user text into SQL — use ? and execute.

weeks.title: Full CRUD: Club Registration App
weeks.goal: I can read, update and delete members with PDO to finish a simple CRUD app.
weeks.learn: CRUD means Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four jobs of every register. Last week we did Create. Now we READ all members in a loop, show a 'Delete' link for each, and UPDATE a member's club. It's like a club secretary who can add, view, correct and remove names.

research.q: Ask a club secretary or class captain: what mistakes do they fix in the register most often?
research.tip: Write the common mistakes — your Update feature should fix them.

build.task: List all members with a Delete link and a quick 'Move to Coding' update.
steps: Connect with PDO (same as last week).
If ?del=id, run a prepared DELETE.
If ?move=id, run a prepared UPDATE.
SELECT all and loop with foreach to show the table.
build.code:
prepare("DELETE FROM members WHERE id = ?")->execute([(int)$_GET["del"]]); } if (isset($_GET["move"])) { $pdo->prepare("UPDATE members SET club = 'Coding' WHERE id = ?")->execute([(int)$_GET["move"]]); } $rows = $pdo->query("SELECT * FROM members ORDER BY club, nickname")->fetchAll(PDO::FETCH_ASSOC); ?>

weeks.title: Hello Python: print and Variables
weeks.goal: I can write Python that prints messages and stores data in variables.
weeks.learn: Python is a friendly language that reads almost like English. 'print()' shows a message on the screen. A variable is a labelled container, like a 'Sugar' tin in the kitchen. In Python you don't need $ or semicolons — just name = value. Indentation (spaces) matters a lot in Python.

research.q: Ask an adult who uses a computer at work: have they heard of Python, and what is it used for?
research.tip: Write their answer — Python is used in many real jobs, from data to AI.

build.task: Write a Python welcome card for the Coding Club using variables.
steps: Store club name, meeting day and number of members in variables.
Use print to show each one.
Use an f-string to join words and variables.
Run it in IDLE or an online Python editor.
build.code:
club = "ByteBusters Coding Club"
school = "Yewa College, Ilaro"
day = "Wednesday"
members = 24

print("Welcome to the", club)
print(f"We meet every {day} at {school}.")
print(f"We have {members} members.")

members = members + 1
print(f"A new member joined! Now we are {members}.")

check.q: What does print() do?
opts: Shows a message on the screen

check.q: In Python, a variable is made with…
What does the f in f"...{day}..." let you do?

weeks.say: I wrote Python that stores club info in variables and prints a welcome card.

trainer.open: We've spoken PHP, JavaScript and SQL. Today we learn the language that reads almost like English — Python!

weeks.title: Python Data Types & Lists
weeks.goal: I can use Python's main data types — int, float, str, bool — and lists.
weeks.learn: Data comes in types, like how a market has items sold by count, by weight or by name. int is a whole number (24 members). float has a point (₦1,500.50). str is text ('Coding'). bool is True or False. A list holds many items in order, like a shopping list. type() tells you what type something is.

research.q: Ask a trader: what do they sell by count (how many) and what by measure (how much)?
research.tip: Write 2 examples of each — count is like int, measure is like float.

build.task: Store club data in different types and a list, then print their types.
steps: Make one int, one float, one str and one bool.
Print each with type().
Make a list of club names.
Use len(), append() and index [0].
build.code:
members = 24                 # int
dues = 200.50                # float (naira)
club = "Coding"              # str
meets_today = True           # bool

print(type(members), type(dues), type(club), type(meets_today))

clubs = ["Coding", "Press", "JETS"]
clubs.append("Drama")
print("Clubs:", clubs)
print("First club:", clubs[0])
print("Number of clubs:", len(clubs))

total_dues = members * dues
print(f"Total dues: ₦{total_dues}")

check.q: Which type is 200.50?
What does clubs[0] give?

opts: Adds an item at the end

weeks.title: Python Rules & Loops: Club Counter
weeks.goal: I can use if/elif/else and for loops to count and check club members.
weeks.learn: Conditionals are rules: IF the club is full, say 'No space', ELSE say 'Welcome'. Loops repeat work, like a teacher calling every name on the register. 'for' goes through each item in a list. Together they let us count members in each club quickly — just like our PHP app, but in Python.

research.q: Ask a club patron: what is the most members a club can take, and why?
research.tip: Write the limit and reason — use it as the 'full' rule in your program.

build.task: Write a Python program that counts members per club and says if each club is full.
steps: Make a list of members' clubs.
Loop with for to count each club in a dictionary.
Use if/elif/else to check full, almost full or open.
Print a neat report.

check.q: Which keyword checks a second rule after if?

opts: Goes through each item in the list

weeks.say: I used Python loops to count club members and if/elif/else rules to say which clubs are full.
